desc:
You may swap two elements of nums (at any two different positions) whenever the absolute difference of their values is at most limit. You can perform any number of swaps.

Return the lexicographically smallest array that can be produced. (Array x is smaller than y if at the first position where they differ, x has the smaller value.)

nums = [1,5,3,9,8], limit = 2          -> [1,3,5,8,9]
nums = [1,7,6,18,2,1], limit = 3        -> [1,6,7,18,1,2]
nums = [1,7,28,19,10], limit = 3        -> [1,7,28,19,10]   (no two values are close enough)
hints: Which pairs of values can trade places? If 1 can swap with 3 and 3 can swap with 5, can 1 and 5 end up exchanged?

Sort the values. Neighbouring values in sorted order that differ by at most limit are linked; a chain of such links forms a block of values that can be rearranged in any order among the positions that hold them.
Sort indices by value and cut the sorted order wherever the gap exceeds limit. For each block, sort its positions and its values, then put the smallest value at the smallest position, and so on.
editorial: Two values within limit can swap, and swapping along a chain of such neighbours lets any value of a block reach any position occupied by the block (just like bubble sort along a path). So the sorted values split into maximal runs where consecutive values differ by at most limit; values of different runs can never interact, and each run owns a fixed set of positions.

Inside a run any arrangement is reachable, so the best arrangement puts the run's values in increasing order on the run's positions in increasing order, making each earlier position as small as possible. Sort the indices by value (O(n log n)), split into runs, sort the positions of each run, and write back. A union-find over the sorted order does the same job as the run split.
